 Modi presses India Inc to raise wages, create jobs 
 The prime minister questioned whether businesses had passed on the benefits of government reforms to employees and urged companies to invest in domestic manufacturing and expand into overseas markets
[Source photo: A video grab from PM Modi's address ]
 More Like This

By PRESS Insider Staff 
 6 minutes 
 Prime Minister Narendra Modi challenged Indian businesses on Thursday, 19 November, to explain whether successive tax cuts and economic reforms had translated into higher wages and more jobs, calling on companies to take greater responsibility for the country’s economic growth.
 Addressing the centenary convention of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, Modi questioned whether companies had done enough to reward workers and expand their operations despite years of government support.
 “Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees?” Modi asked, referring to the government’s decision to lower the basic corporate tax rate from 30% to 22%.
 The remarks come as industry associations prepare their recommendations for the next Union budget, with businesses seeking further policy support, tax concessions and regulatory reforms.
 Modi said the government remained open to suggestions from industry but urged businesses to examine their own contribution to employment, household incomes, manufacturing and exports.
 Seven years after the corporate tax cut
 In September 2019, the government introduced one of India’s biggest corporate tax reforms, allowing domestic companies to pay a basic tax rate of 22%, down from 30%, provided they forgo certain exemptions and incentives.
 Eligible new manufacturing companies were offered a concessional rate of 15% to attract fresh investment, expand industrial capacity and strengthen India’s position as a global manufacturing destination.
 The finance ministry at the time estimated the annual revenue forgone from the corporate tax reductions and accompanying fiscal measures at ₹1.45 trillion, or ₹1,45,000 crore.
 Modi also pointed to the personal income tax changes announced in the 2025-26 Union budget, under which individuals earning up to ₹12 lakh annually became eligible for zero tax liability on ordinary income under the new tax regime.
 Combined with reductions in goods and services tax (GST) rates on several products and improvements in tax administration, these measures were intended to strengthen household purchasing power and stimulate consumer demand.
 The prime minister questioned whether businesses had responded adequately to these concessions by increasing employee compensation or expanding their workforce.
 Corporate profits and the wage gap
 The relationship between corporate profitability and employee incomes has been a concern within the government for several years.
 The Economic Survey 2024-25 highlighted a widening disparity between corporate earnings and employment growth.
 Corporate profits rose 22.3% in fiscal 2024, while employment increased by just 1.5%, according to the survey. Corporate profits as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) reached a 15-year high of 4.8%.
 The survey warned that weak wage growth could constrain household consumption and undermine the sustainability of economic expansion.
 More recent Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, covering 4,278 listed non-government, non-financial companies, showed a mixed picture across industries in fiscal 2026.
 Manufacturing companies recorded a 10.3% increase in operating profits, compared with 6% in the previous financial year, while staff costs increased by 10.7%.
 At information technology companies, operating profits grew 10.7%, compared with a 6.1% increase in staff expenditure. Non-IT services companies recorded a 7.1% increase in operating profits and a 9% rise in staff costs.
 Employee expenditure as a proportion of sales remained broadly unchanged in manufacturing but declined among services companies.
 Aggregate staff expenditure, however, does not necessarily indicate individual salary increases or net additions to company payrolls.
 The distribution of corporate earnings has wider economic implications for India, where household consumption accounts for the largest share of economic activity. Weak income growth can restrict demand for discretionary goods and services, in turn affecting businesses’ willingness to invest in additional capacity.
 Employment improves but challenges remain
 Modi’s remarks came days after the release of official employment data showing a modest improvement in India’s labor market.
 The unemployment rate among people aged 15 and above declined to 4.9% in October from 5% in September and 5.2% a year earlier, according to the Periodic Labour Force Survey, released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation on 16 November.
 Urban unemployment stood at 6.7%, compared with 4.2% in rural areas.
 The proportion of the working-age population in employment increased to 53% in October from 52.5% a year ago, while female labor force participation rose to 35% from 34.2%.
 Despite the improvement, unemployment among urban women remained relatively high at 8.7%.
 The figures capture employment across the economy, including self-employment, agriculture and informal work, and do not necessarily reflect the availability of regular salaried jobs.
 The government has also introduced direct financial incentives to encourage formal-sector employment.
 The Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana, approved in July 2025 with an allocation of ₹99,446 crore, aims to support the creation of more than 35 million jobs over two years, with particular emphasis on manufacturing.
 The program provides financial assistance to eligible first-time employees and employers that expand their workforce. It covers jobs created between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027.
 Modi calls for more domestic manufacturing
 Beyond employment and wages, Modi urged businesses to reconsider their dependence on imported industrial inputs and identify opportunities to manufacture higher-value products in India.
 He cited pharmaceuticals, metals, food processing and engineering equipment as industries where India has established strengths but remains dependent on imports or has yet to secure a significant share of global markets.
 India is a major supplier of finished pharmaceutical products, but domestic drugmakers continue to depend on imported ingredients for several medicines. Modi called for investment in the production of these inputs to strengthen pharmaceutical supply chains.
 He also pointed to the contradiction of India exporting iron ore while importing certain grades of finished steel, and possessing substantial bauxite reserves while relying on overseas suppliers for specialized aluminum products.
 In agriculture, Modi noted that India accounted for only about 2-2.5% of global agricultural exports despite its vast production base.
 Processed food’s share of India’s agricultural and food exports had increased from 13% to more than 20% over the past 12 years, he said, calling for greater investment in food processing, procurement networks and products suited to international demand.
 Modi also identified hand tools, power tools, packaging equipment, irrigation systems and industrial machinery as areas where Indian manufacturers could expand their presence in developing economies.
 Trade agreements offer new markets
 The prime minister questioned whether Indian companies had developed concrete plans to capitalize on the country’s growing network of free trade agreements (FTAs), including those with major developed economies.
 He urged businesses to invest in understanding overseas consumers, meeting international product standards and establishing distribution networks rather than relying predominantly on domestic demand.
 India has pursued closer trade ties with several major economies in recent years as it seeks to diversify export markets, attract investment and increase its participation in international supply chains.
 However, preferential access to foreign markets does not automatically translate into higher exports. Companies must also meet rules of origin, regulatory requirements and quality standards while remaining competitive on price and delivery.
 Modi said FICCI could help develop an industry-wide strategy to make better use of the trade agreements negotiated by the government.
 He also cautioned companies against treating India’s population of more than 1.4 billion as a guaranteed market for their products.
 “Our domestic market should not be our comfort zone,” Modi said, according to the Prime Minister’s Office.
 He urged manufacturers to apply the same standards to products sold in India as those destined for overseas markets.
 Private investment remains central to growth
 The appeal to businesses comes as the government seeks greater private-sector participation in sustaining India’s economic expansion after several years of substantial public investment in infrastructure.
 India’s economy grew 7.8% in fiscal 2026, according to an RBI study on private corporate investment published last month.
 The study noted that strong domestic demand, healthy bank balance sheets and sustained capital expenditure supported investment prospects, although global economic uncertainties continued to weigh on the near-term outlook.
 For the government, attracting investment into industries that generate large numbers of jobs remains particularly important. Capital-intensive sectors can contribute substantially to economic output and exports without generating employment on the scale required by India’s expanding workforce.
 Industries such as textiles, food processing, footwear, tourism and light engineering offer opportunities to absorb workers across a broader range of skill and education levels.
